

\section{Heisenberg Groups}

\subsection{The CR Structures on the Heisenberg Group }
\begin{definition}[cf. \cite{folland_estimates_1974}]
    The \textbf{Heisenberg group} (of degree \( n \)) is the Lie group \( H_n \) whose underlying manifold is \( \mathbb{C}^n \times \mathbb{R} \) with coordinates \( (z_1, \ldots, z_n, t) \equiv (z, t) \) and whose group law is given by
\[
(z, t) \cdot (z', t') = (z + z', t + t' + 2 \Im ( z \cdot z')), \quad z \cdot z' = \sum_{i=1}^n z_i \overline{z'_i}.
\]

\end{definition}

If we set \( z_j = x_j + iy_j \), then \( (x_1, \ldots, x_n, y_1, \ldots, y_n, t) \) form a real coordinate system for \( H_n \). In this coordinate system we define the following vector fields:
\begin{equation}
X_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} + 2y_j \frac{\partial}{\partial t}, \quad Y_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial y_j} - 2x_j \frac{\partial}{\partial t}, \quad T = \frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\end{equation}

It is a simple exercise to verify that \( \{X_1, \ldots, X_n, Y_1, \ldots, Y_n, T\} \) is a basis for the \textbf{left-invariant vector fields} on \( H_n \). The commutation relations are as follows:

\begin{equation}
[Y_j, X_k] = 4\delta_{jk} T, \quad [X_j, X_k] = [Y_j, Y_k] = [X_j, T] = [Y_j, T] = 0.
\end{equation}
\begin{remark}
    Note that these are an abstract form of the commutation relations for the quantum-mechanical position and momentum operators in $n$-space; hence the name ``Heisenberg group''.
\end{remark}
\begin{remark}
    If one use 
    \[X_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} + \frac{1}{2}y_j \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\]
    to define the distribution, then they are not left-invariant. And the Levi form $\tau$ defined below has to be changed.
\end{remark}


We further define the complex vector fields
\begin{equation}
Z_j = \frac{1}{2}(X_j - iY_j) = \frac{\partial}{\partial z_j} + i \bar{z}_j\frac{\partial}{\partial t}, \quad \overline{Z}_j = \frac{1}{2}(X_j + iY_j) = \frac{\partial}{\partial \overline{z}_j} - iz_j\frac{\partial}{\partial t}
\end{equation}
whose commutation relations are
\begin{equation}
[Z_j, \overline{Z}_k] = -2i\delta_{jk} T, \quad [Z_j, Z_k] = [\overline{Z}_j, \overline{Z}_k] = [Z_j, T] = [\overline{Z}_j, T] = 0,
\end{equation}
and the one-form
\begin{equation}\label{eq5}
\tau = dt + 2 \sum_{j=1}^n (x_j \, dy_j - y_j \, dx_j).
\end{equation}
We note that \( \langle \tau, Z_j \rangle = \langle \tau, \overline{Z}_j \rangle = 0 \) for all \( j \). It is immediate that the subbundle \( T^{1,0} \) of \( \mathbb{C}T H_n \) spanned by \( Z_1, \ldots, Z_n \) defines a CR structure on \( H_n \). To compute the Lévi form, we have
\[
\langle Z_j, Z_k \rangle_L = \frac{1}{2i}\langle \tau, [Z_j, \overline{Z}_k] \rangle = \frac{1}{2i}(\tau, -2i\delta_{jk} T) = \delta_{jk}.
\]
Thus \( H_n \) is \textbf{strongly pseudoconvex}.

\begin{remark}
    \(\eqref{eq5}\) is equal to (cf. \cite{dragomir_differential_2006})
    \begin{equation}
    \theta_0 = dt + i \sum_{j=1}^n \left( z^j d\overline{z}^j - \overline{z}^j dz^j \right)
    \end{equation}
in complex form, and by differentiating it  we obtain
\begin{equation}
d\theta_0 = 2i \sum_{j=1}^n dz^j \wedge d\overline{z}^j.
\end{equation}
\end{remark}

\subsection{A geometrical interpretation}
This has the following geometrical interpretation due to Pyatetski-Shapiro. Set
\[
D_{n+1} = \left\{ \zeta \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} : \sum_{j=1}^n |\zeta_j|^2 - \Im  \zeta_0 < 0 \right\},
\]
\[
M_n = \partial D_{n+1} = \left\{ \zeta \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} : \sum_{j=1}^n |\zeta_j|^2 = \Im  \zeta_0 \right\}.
\]
\(D_{n+1}\) (known as the \textit{Siegel domain}) is holomorphically equivalent to the unit ball in \(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\). \(H_n\) acts on \(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\) by holomorphic affine transformations which preserve \(D_{n+1}\) and \(M_n\), as follows: if \((z,t) \in H_n\) and \(\zeta \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1}\), \((z,t) \cdot \zeta = \zeta'\), where
\[
\zeta_0' = \zeta_0 + t + i |z|^2 + 2i \sum_{j=1}^n \zeta_j \overline{z}_j,
\]
\[
\zeta_j' = \zeta_j + z_j, \quad j > 0.
\]
\(H_n\) acts simply transitively on \(M_n\) and so may be identified with \(M_n\) via the correspondence
\[
(z,t) \longleftrightarrow (z,t) \cdot 0 = (t + i|z|^2, z_1, \ldots, z_n).
\]
Under this identification, the CR structure on \(H_n\) described above coincides with the CR structure on \(M_n\) induced from \(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\). (Indeed, one easily checks that the holomorphic subspaces at the origin are the same since \(M_n\) is tangent to the hyperplane \(\zeta_0 = 0\) there. But the CR structure on \(H_n\) is left-invariant, and the action of \(H_n\) on \(M_n\), being holomorphic, preserves the CR structure on \(M_n\); hence the holomorphic subspaces coincide everywhere.)

\begin{remark}
    The action is \textbf{simply transitive} (or sharply transitive, or regular) if it is both transitive and free (cf. \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_action}{wikipedia}).
\end{remark}

\subsection{Another useful identification}

Another useful identification is that of the Heisenberg group and the sphere $S^{2n+1} \subset \mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ minus a point. 

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^{N}$ be a domain with smooth boundary $\partial \Omega$, i.e., there is an open neighborhood $U$ of the closure $\overline{\Omega}$ in $\mathbb{C}$ and a $C^\infty$ function $\rho \colon U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\Omega = \{ x \in U \colon \rho(x) > 0\}$ (and $\partial \Omega = \{ x \in U \colon \rho(x) = 0\}$) and $(D\rho)_x \neq 0$ at any $x \in \partial \Omega$. Let $T_{1,0}(\partial \Omega)$ be the induced CR structure on $\partial \Omega$, as a real hypersurface in $\mathbb{C}^N$. Let $\theta$ be the pullback to $\partial \Omega$ of the real $1$-form $i(\bar{\partial} - \partial)\rho$ on $U$. Then $\theta$ is a pseudo-Hermitian structure on $(\partial \Omega, T_{1,0}(\partial \Omega))$. As we just saw, the boundary of the Siegel domain is a strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold. 
\begin{proof}
From
    \[\partial\rho = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j} - i\frac{\partial}{\partial y_j} \right)\rho (dx_j+idy_j)
    \]
    we know
    \[i(\bar{\partial} - \partial)\rho=\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x_j}dy_j-\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial y_j}dx_j.
    \]
    Now it's easy to verify 
    \[
    \theta(J(\nabla \rho))=|\nabla \rho|^2\neq 0, \; \theta(T_j)=0, \forall T_j \perp \{\nabla \rho, J\nabla\rho\}.
    \]
\end{proof}

Also, the sphere $S^{2n+1} \subset \mathbb{C}^{2n+1}$ is a strictly pseudoconvex manifold, since the boundary of the unit ball $B_{n+1} = \{ z \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} \colon |z| < 1 \}$, and the (restriction to $S^{2n+1} \setminus \{p\}$ of the) Cayley transform (cf. Friedrich Haslinger's notes.)
 $$\Phi(z_1, \ldots, z_n,z_{n+1}) = (w_1, \ldots, w_n, w_{n+1}), $$
$\text{ where } w_j = \frac{z_j}{(1 + z_n)} \text{ for } 1 \leq j \leq n \text{ and } w_{n+1} = i\frac{(1 - z_{n+1})}{(1 + z_{n+1})} .$ This gives a CR isomorphism $S^{2n+1} \setminus \{p\} \cong \partial \Omega_{2n+1}$ (and thus a CR isomorphism $S^{2n+1} \setminus \{p\} \cong H_n$).



\subsection{A left-invariant \(k\)-strongly pseudoconvex CR structure}
We can also define a left-invariant CR structure on \(H_n\) which is \(k\)-strongly pseudoconvex, \(\frac{n}{2} \leq k \leq n\), by taking \(T_{1,0}\) to be the bundle spanned by \(Z_1, \ldots, Z_k, \overline{Z}_{k+1}, \ldots, \overline{Z}_n\). A few words of explanation about this will be helpful. Let us take \((w_1, \ldots, w_n, t)\) as new coordinates on \(H_n\), where \(w_j = z_j, 1 \leq j \leq k\), and \(w_j = \overline{z}_j, k + 1 \leq j \leq n\). Set \(\varepsilon_j = 1\) or \(-1\) according as \(j \leq k\) or \(j > k\), and define the Hermitian form \(Q_k\) on \(\mathbb{C}^n\) by
\[
Q_k(w, w') = \sum_{j=1}^n \varepsilon_j w_j \overline{w}'_j.
\]
Then in the coordinates \((w, t)\) the group law is
\[
(w, t)(w', t') = (w + w', t + t' + 2\Im Q_k(w, w')).
\]

The left-invariant vector field agreeing with \(\frac{\partial}{\partial w_j}\) at the origin is
\begin{equation}
W_j = \frac{\partial}{\partial w_j} + \varepsilon_j i\overline{w}_j \frac{\partial}{\partial t'},
\end{equation}
and \(T_{1,0}\) is the bundle spanned by \(W_1, \ldots, W_n\). In fact, \(W_j = Z_j, j \leq k\), and \(W_j = \overline{Z}_j, j > k\). As above, the Levi form is given by \(\langle W_j, W_l \rangle_L = \varepsilon_j \delta_{jl}\). The geometrical realization of \(H_n\) also has an analogue here: \(H_n\) may be embedded in \(\mathbb{C}^{n+1}\) as the hypersurface
\begin{equation}
\{\zeta \in \mathbb{C}^{n+1} : \Im  \zeta_0 = Q_k(\zeta', \zeta')\}, \quad \zeta' = (\zeta_1, \ldots, \zeta_n),
\end{equation}
via the mapping
\[
(w, t) \mapsto (t + i Q_k(w, w), w_1, \ldots, w_n)
\]
which preserves the CR structure.

\subsection{Unsolvable Operators}
At this point we should also mention that, in the case $n=1$, the vector field $\bar{Z} = (\partial/\partial z) - i z (\partial/\partial t)$ which spans $T_{0,1}$ is the unsolvable operator of H. Lewy. Indeed, Lewy was led to this phenomenon by considering boundary values of holomorphic functions on $D_2$.
\begin{theorem}[cf. \cite{john_partial_1982}]
Let $L$ denote the differential operator acting on functions $u(x,y,z)$ defined by
\begin{equation}
Lu = -u_x - iu_y + 2i(x + iy)u_z. \tag{1.1a}
\end{equation}
There exists a function $F(x,y,z) \in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)$ such that the equation
\begin{equation}
Lu = F(x,y,z) \tag{1.1b}
\end{equation}
has no solution whose domain is an open set $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with $u \in C^1(\Omega)$, and $u_x, u_y, u_z$ H\"older continuous in $\Omega$.
\end{theorem}
